Sampled HR@10 can obscure full-catalog ranking failures: Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; smaller candidate pools also make different ranking metrics increasingly resemble AUC. Large margins against random training negatives therefore do not establish strong top-10 ranking. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/). RecSys 2025 research distinguishes sampling reliability through resolution, fidelity, robustness and predictive power, emphasizing that exposure bias and candidate sampling both affect conclusions. [Sampling Reliability](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086).

Popularity-stratified analysis is particularly relevant. A 2024 sequential-recommendation study found aggregate performance concealed head/mid/tail imbalances: random negative sampling favored head items, while popularity-based sampling produced more balanced performance with an overall accuracy tradeoff. These are dataset-dependent findings, not evidence that changing the sampler necessarily helps BERT4Rec here. [Performance and Bias of Negative Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276).

Suggested diagnostic inference: freeze the single trained BERT4Rec per category and audit identical public training-prefix targets against both fixed sampled candidates and the eligible full catalog, masking prefix-seen items. Record target ranks, sampled/full hit disagreement, target score minus the tenth-highest competing score, and the tenth–eleventh score gap; stratify by prefix-derived item frequency and history length. This separates easy-negative margins from competition near the top-10 boundary. Treat unobserved items as unlabeled competitors, not verified dislikes. Training-prefix audits remain in-sample diagnostics; preserve the host’s validation candidates, seeds and macro HR@10 selection unchanged.
